decks.title: Water as a Universal Solvent — Part 1: Water as a solvent, kinds of mixtures and saturated solutions
goals: Explain why water is called a universal solvent
Compare solutions, colloids and suspensions in particle size, stability and visibility
Distinguish unsaturated, saturated and supersaturated solutions and describe how to test one

slides.heading: Water as a Universal Solvent
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what dissolves in water, and how to tell a solution from other mixtures.

visual.alt: Flow: solute and water give a solution

slides.narration: Sugar vanishes in tea. Salt disappears in soup. Water makes this happen for thousands of substances, which is why we call it the universal solvent. Let us see how, and where the name is not quite true.

slides.heading: Why water is a universal solvent
slides.body_md: Water molecules are **polar**: one end is slightly negative and the other slightly positive, so they pull ionic compounds and many polar substances apart.

rows: Common salt, sugar, washing soda, copper sulphate
Ammonia, hydrogen chloride and carbon dioxide gases (to different extents)

visual.alt: Table of substances that dissolve well in water and substances that hardly dissolve

slides.narration: Water dissolves more substances than any other common liquid, including solids, liquids and gases. It dissolves most ionic compounds and many polar substances. But oil, wax and sand do not dissolve, so universal is a strong word.

slides.heading: Quick check: a poor solvent case
slides.body_md: Which of these will **not** dissolve in water to any noticeable extent?
slides.narration: Think of a substance that floats as a separate layer on water.

slides.heading: Solution, colloid or suspension?

rows: About one to one thousand nanometres

visual.alt: Table comparing solutions, colloids and suspensions

slides.narration: Compare the three by particle size. In a solution the particles are tiny and never settle. In a colloid they are larger, scatter light and still never settle. In a suspension they are large, make the liquid cloudy and slowly settle out.

slides.heading: The Tyndall effect
slides.body_md: A narrow beam of light is **scattered** by colloidal particles, so its path shows up in the liquid.

visual.alt: A solution, a colloid and a suspension in a beam of light

slides.narration: Shine a torch through each jar from the side. In the solution the particles are too small to scatter light, so the beam is invisible. In the colloid the beam lights up as a bright path. In the suspension the liquid is cloudy and a layer settles at the bottom.

slides.heading: Quick check: the beam of light
slides.body_md: A liquid looks clear. A torch beam shows a bright path in it, and nothing settles on standing. It is a…
slides.narration: Which mixture scatters light but does not settle?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: sort the mixtures
slides.body_md: Three mixtures are made in water: **P** salt, **Q** powdered chalk, **R** starch paste. P is clear and shows no beam. Q is cloudy and leaves a white layer after an hour. R is almost clear but shows a bright beam and does not settle.
bullets: Step 1: P is clear and shows no beam, so it is a **solution**.
Step 2: Q is cloudy and settles, so it is a **suspension**.
Step 3: R shows a beam but does not settle, so it is a **colloid**.

visual.alt: Worked table sorting three mixtures by their observations

slides.narration: Use the clues one at a time. No beam and clear liquid means a solution. A cloudy liquid that settles is a suspension. A beam of light that is visible while nothing settles means a colloid. Always check both clues.

slides.heading: Solute, solvent and solubility
slides.body_md: A **solution** has a **solute** (the part that dissolves) in a **solvent** (the liquid that dissolves it). **Solubility** is the mass of solute that saturates **100 g of solvent** at a given temperature.

rows: Grams of solute that saturate 100 g of water

visual.alt: Table of the terms solute, solvent, solution and solubility

slides.narration: The substance that dissolves is the solute. The liquid it dissolves in is the solvent. Together they make the solution. Solubility counts how many grams of solute saturate one hundred grams of water at a stated temperature.

slides.heading: Unsaturated, saturated, supersaturated

rows: Can dissolve more solute at that temperature
Holds as much solute as it can at that temperature
Holds more than a saturated solution (unstable)
Extra solute crystallises out at once

visual.alt: Table of the three kinds of solution and the crystal test for each

slides.narration: An unsaturated solution can take more solute. A saturated solution is full at that temperature. A supersaturated solution holds even more than that, but it is unstable. A single crystal makes the extra solid appear.

slides.heading: Testing with a crystal
slides.body_md: Add one small crystal of the **same solute**, stir gently and watch.

slides.narration: Add a single crystal of the same salt to each solution. If it dissolves, the solution was unsaturated. If it stays unchanged, the solution is saturated. If crystals suddenly grow all around it, the solution was supersaturated.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading the test
slides.body_md: A crystal of the same salt dropped into a solution neither dissolves nor grows. The solution is…
slides.narration: The crystal does nothing at all. What does that say about the solution?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how to make a saturated solution
slides.body_md: A student wants a saturated solution of salt at room temperature.
bullets: Step 1: warm or stir water in a beaker and add salt in **small portions**.
Step 2: keep stirring after each portion until it dissolves.
Step 3: stop when a little salt **stays undissolved** after long stirring; decant or filter the clear liquid.
Step 4: confirm it is saturated by adding one more crystal; it does not dissolve.

nodes.label: Add salt in portions and stir

visual.alt: Flow for making and testing a saturated solution

slides.narration: Add the salt a little at a time and stir. When a few grains remain at the bottom after thorough stirring, no more will dissolve at that temperature. Pour off the clear liquid. A fresh crystal will not dissolve, which confirms it.

slides.heading: A supersaturated solution
slides.body_md: Cool a **hot saturated** solution slowly and **without disturbing it**; extra solute may stay dissolved for a while.

visual.alt: Flow from a hot saturated solution to a supersaturated solution that crystallises when disturbed

slides.narration: If a hot saturated solution cools very slowly and is left undisturbed, the extra solute may stay dissolved. This unstable state is called supersaturated. A crystal dropped in, or a knock, sets the extra solute crystallising at once.

slides.heading: Quick check: supersaturation
slides.body_md: True or false: a supersaturated solution is stable and cannot be made to crystallise by adding a crystal.
slides.narration: Is a supersaturated solution stable?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Water dissolves many but not all substances, so it is a universal solvent only in a broad sense.
Solution: tiny particles, clear, no beam, no settling. Colloid: scatters light, no settling. Suspension: cloudy, settles.
Test with a crystal: dissolves is unsaturated, unchanged is saturated, crystals appear is supersaturated.

visual.alt: Summary table of the three mixtures

slides.narration: To recap. Water dissolves a great many substances. Solutions, colloids and suspensions differ in particle size, in whether a beam is visible, and in whether they settle. One crystal tells you whether a solution is unsaturated, saturated or supersaturated.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give **two** differences when asked to distinguish: particle size plus one observation.
Define solubility with **100 g of water** and a **stated temperature**.
In the crystal test, name **both** the observation and the type of solution.
Do not call every clear liquid a solution; check for a beam of light.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Give two differences when you distinguish things. When you define solubility, say one hundred grams of water and the temperature. In the crystal test, give the observation and the conclusion. And remember that a clear liquid is not always a solution.

slides.heading: Solubility Curves
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how temperature changes the amount that dissolves, and what the curves tell us.

visual.alt: Flow: temperature, solubility, curve

slides.narration: A hot drink dissolves more sugar than a cold one. But not every solid behaves like sugar. A solubility curve shows the full story for one substance, in a single picture.

slides.heading: Reading solubility
slides.body_md: Solubility is measured in **grams of solute per 100 grams of water** at a stated temperature. A solubility curve plots it against temperature.

slides.narration: This table gives grams of solute per hundred grams of water. The numbers are rounded and illustrative, in the shape textbooks draw. Notice how fast potassium nitrate changes, and how little sodium chloride does.

slides.heading: The three curves

slides.heading: Quick check: reading a curve
slides.body_md: From the curves, the solubility of potassium nitrate at sixty degrees Celsius is closest to…
slides.narration: Go up from sixty on the temperature axis to the red curve, then across.

slides.heading: Three behaviours

rows: Very low; slight rise then fall
Slightly soluble; falls a little in hot water

visual.alt: Table of the three behaviours of solubility curves

slides.narration: Three behaviours. Potassium nitrate becomes far more soluble when heated. Sodium chloride hardly changes. Calcium sulphate is only slightly soluble and gets a little less soluble in very hot water.

slides.heading: Quick check: sodium chloride
slides.body_md: Which statement about sodium chloride is correct?
slides.narration: Look at the shape of the blue curve.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how much dissolves?
slides.body_md: Potassium nitrate has a solubility of 110 g per 100 g of water at 60 °C. How much dissolves in 50 g of water to make a saturated solution, and what is the mass of that solution?
bullets: Step 1: 110 g saturate 100 g, so for 50 g: 110 × 50 ÷ 100 = 55 g.
Step 2: mass of solution = water + solute = 50 + 55 = 105 g.

visual.alt: Worked table: fifty grams of water dissolves fifty-five grams and makes one hundred and five grams of solution

slides.narration: Scale the solubility to the water you have. One hundred grams of water takes one hundred and ten grams, so fifty grams takes fifty five grams. Then add the water and the solute to get the mass of the solution, one hundred and five grams.

slides.heading: Cooling a hot saturated solution
slides.body_md: Because potassium nitrate is much less soluble when cold, the **excess crystallises out** as the solution cools.

visual.alt: Flow from a hot saturated solution, cooling, lower solubility, crystals forming and filtering

slides.narration: A hot saturated solution of potassium nitrate holds a lot. As it cools, the solubility falls, so the solution can no longer hold it all. The extra comes out as crystals, which you can filter off.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: crystals on cooling
slides.body_md: A saturated solution is made with 200 g of water at 80 °C and cooled to 20 °C. (Solubility of potassium nitrate: 169 g at 80 °C and 32 g at 20 °C per 100 g of water.)
bullets: Step 1: at 80 °C, 200 g of water holds 169 × 200 ÷ 100 = 338 g.
Step 2: at 20 °C it can hold only 32 × 200 ÷ 100 = 64 g.
Step 3: crystals formed = 338 − 64 = 274 g.

visual.alt: Worked table: three hundred and thirty-eight grams at eighty degrees, sixty-four at twenty, so two hundred and seventy-four grams of crystals

slides.narration: Find what the water holds at each temperature, then subtract. At the higher temperature it holds three hundred and thirty eight grams. At the lower temperature it holds only sixty four grams. The difference, two hundred and seventy four grams, comes out as crystals.

slides.heading: Quick check: why crystals appear
slides.body_md: Why do crystals of potassium nitrate form when its hot saturated solution cools?
slides.narration: What happens to the solubility as the temperature falls?

slides.heading: Worked example 3: saturated or not?
slides.body_md: 40 g of potassium nitrate is stirred into 50 g of water at 40 °C. (Solubility at 40 °C: 64 g per 100 g of water.)
bullets: Step 1: the most that dissolves in 50 g of water = 64 × 50 ÷ 100 = 32 g.
Step 2: 40 g is more than 32 g, so the solution is **saturated**.
Step 3: undissolved solid = 40 − 32 = 8 g.

visual.alt: Worked table: forty grams added, thirty-two grams dissolve, eight grams left

slides.narration: Work out the most the water can hold. It is thirty two grams. You added forty, which is more, so the solution is saturated and eight grams stays undissolved at the bottom.

slides.heading: Separating two salts by cooling
slides.body_md: Cool a hot saturated mixture of potassium nitrate and sodium chloride. Mostly **potassium nitrate** crystallises, because sodium chloride changes so little with temperature.

visual.alt: Table of the mass of each salt that crystallises from one hundred grams of water on cooling from sixty to twenty degrees

slides.narration: The two curves behave very differently. On cooling from sixty to twenty degrees, about seventy eight grams of potassium nitrate come out of a hundred grams of water, but only about one gram of sodium chloride. Cooling separates them.

slides.heading: Quick check: calcium sulphate
slides.body_md: True or false: calcium sulphate is highly soluble and its solubility rises steeply with temperature.
slides.narration: Why did it need its own small graph?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Solubility is grams of solute per 100 g of water at a stated temperature.
Potassium nitrate: steep rise. Sodium chloride: nearly flat. Calcium sulphate: very low.
Solute in a mass of water = solubility × water ÷ 100.
Cooling a hot saturated solution of potassium nitrate makes crystals.

rows: Held when hot minus held when cold

visual.alt: Summary table of two calculation methods

slides.narration: To recap. Read the curve at the stated temperature. Scale the solubility to your mass of water. To find crystals formed on cooling, subtract what the water holds when cold from what it held when hot.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Read the graph at the **exact temperature**; draw dotted lines to the axes.
Show **each step** and include the unit, g per 100 g of water.
Compare curves by **steepness**: say which one rises steeply and which hardly changes.
Note when a table or graph says its data are **illustrative**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Read the graph at the exact temperature and draw guide lines. Show every step of a calculation and keep the unit. Compare curves by steepness. And use the data you are given, not numbers you remember.

sections.heading: 1. Water as a universal solvent; solutions, colloids and suspensions
sections.body_md:
Water dissolves more substances than any other common liquid (solids such as salt and sugar, liquids such as alcohol, and gases such as ammonia), so it is called the **universal solvent**. Its molecules are **polar**, which lets them pull ionic and polar substances apart. The name is not strictly true: oils, wax and sand do not dissolve in water.

A **solution** has a **solute** dissolved in a **solvent**. Mixtures of a solid or liquid in water are classed by particle size.

| Property | Solution | Colloid | Suspension |
|---|---|---|---|
| Particle size | Smaller than about 1 nm | About 1 nm to 1000 nm | Larger than about 1000 nm |
| Appearance | Clear | Clear or slightly cloudy | Cloudy |
| Settles on standing? | No | No | Yes |
| Tyndall effect (beam of light seen)? | No | Yes | Yes (cloudy liquid) |
| Passes through filter paper? | Yes | Yes | No |
| Example | Sugar or salt in water | Milk, starch in water | Chalk powder in water |

The **Tyndall effect** is the scattering of a beam of light by colloidal particles so that the path of the beam is seen. The size limits are approximate; books quote them slightly differently.

key_terms.definition_md: The substance that dissolves in a solution.
The liquid in which the solute dissolves.
A mixture with particles large enough to scatter light but too small to settle.
A cloudy mixture whose large particles settle on standing.

sections.heading: 2. Saturated, unsaturated and supersaturated solutions
sections.body_md:
**Solubility** of a solid in water is the **mass of the solid, in grams, that saturates 100 g of water at a stated temperature**.

| Type | Meaning | Test with a crystal of the solute |
|---|---|---|
| **Unsaturated** | Can still dissolve more solute at that temperature | The crystal dissolves |
| **Saturated** | Holds as much solute as it can at that temperature | The crystal stays unchanged |
| **Supersaturated** | Holds more than a saturated solution at that temperature (unstable) | Extra solute crystallises out at once |

**Making a saturated solution:** add the solute in small portions to water, stirring after each portion, until a little stays undissolved; pour off or filter the clear liquid.

**Making a supersaturated solution:** cool a hot saturated solution slowly and undisturbed. A crystal added or a knock makes the excess crystallise.

If a solution is saturated, more solute dissolves only if the temperature is raised (for most solids).

key_terms.definition_md: Grams of solute that saturate 100 g of water at a given temperature.
A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature.
An unstable solution that holds more solute than it normally could at that temperature.

sections.heading: 3. Effect of temperature on solubility; solubility curves
sections.body_md:
A **solubility curve** plots solubility (g per 100 g of water) against temperature.

| Temperature (°C) | Potassium nitrate | Sodium chloride |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | 32 | 36 |
| 40 | 64 | 37 |
| 60 | 110 | 37 |
| 80 | 169 | 38 |

- **Potassium nitrate:** solubility **rises steeply** with temperature.
- **Sodium chloride:** solubility changes **very little** (curve almost flat).
- **Calcium sulphate:** only **slightly soluble**; its solubility is very small and decreases a little at higher temperatures.

**Crystallisation on cooling:** a hot saturated solution of potassium nitrate cools, its solubility falls, and the **excess crystallises out**. For example, a saturated solution made with 200 g of water at 80 °C gives 274 g of crystals when cooled to 20 °C.

**Calculations:** solute in a given water = solubility × water ÷ 100. Crystals formed = solute held when hot − solute held when cold.

**All numbers in this chapter's tables and graphs are rounded, illustrative values in the shape of textbook curves, not laboratory measurements.**

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Defining solubility without **100 g of water** or without a **temperature**.
- Saying a clear liquid is always a solution; a colloid can also look clear, so check the **beam of light**.
- Saying "the solution becomes saturated" in the crystal test without stating the **observation** (crystal dissolves, stays, or crystals appear).
- Forgetting to **scale** the solubility to the actual mass of water.
- Reading the graph at the wrong temperature; draw **dotted guide lines** to both axes.
- Saying all solids dissolve more in hot water; sodium chloride hardly changes and calcium sulphate falls slightly.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, a definition word, or a reading from the graph.
- 2 marks: two differences or two observations, matched point for point.
- 3 marks: a short numerical with working, or a comparison of three curves.
- 10-mark structured question: a situation or graph followed by parts such as a calculation, a reading, an explanation and a labelled diagram.

cards.front_md: Why is water called the universal solvent?
cards.back_md: It dissolves more substances than any other common liquid.

cards.front_md: Why can water dissolve ionic compounds?
cards.back_md: Its molecules are polar and pull the ions apart.

cards.front_md: Two substances that do not dissolve in water?
cards.back_md: Cooking oil and wax (sand also).
The substance that dissolves.

Smaller than about 1 nanometre.
About 1 to 1000 nanometres.
Larger than about 1000 nanometres.

Scattering of a light beam by colloidal particles so the path is seen.
Milk (or starch in water).

cards.front_md: Does a solution pass through filter paper?
cards.back_md: Yes. A suspension does not.
Grams of solute that saturate 100 g of water at a given temperature.

Cannot dissolve more solute at that temperature.
Holds more solute than a saturated solution; unstable.

The solution is saturated.

cards.front_md: Crystal test: crystals appear at once means?
cards.back_md: The solution is supersaturated.

cards.front_md: How is a saturated solution prepared?
cards.back_md: Add solute in small portions with stirring until a little stays undissolved.

cards.front_md: How can a supersaturated solution be made?
cards.back_md: Cool a hot saturated solution slowly and undisturbed.

cards.back_md: Rises steeply with temperature.

cards.front_md: Shape of the sodium chloride curve?
cards.back_md: Almost flat.
Very small; falls slightly at higher temperatures.

cards.front_md: Why does potassium nitrate crystallise on cooling?
cards.back_md: Its solubility falls, so the excess comes out.

cards.front_md: Solute dissolved in a given mass of water?
cards.back_md: Solubility × mass of water ÷ 100.

cards.front_md: Best way to separate potassium nitrate from sodium chloride in a hot mixture?
cards.back_md: Cool it: mostly potassium nitrate crystallises.

questions.stem_md: Which of these will not dissolve in water to any noticeable extent?
questions.solution_md: Oil is not polar enough to be pulled apart by water and floats as a layer — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A liquid looks clear. A torch beam shows a bright path in it, and nothing settles on standing. It is a
questions.solution_md: A visible beam with no settling means light is scattered by particles that are small enough to stay afloat: a colloid — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A crystal of the same salt dropped into a solution neither dissolves nor grows. The solution is
questions.solution_md: No change means the solution holds all it can at that temperature — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A supersaturated solution is stable and cannot be made to crystallise by adding a crystal.
questions.solution_md: False. It is unstable: a crystal or a knock makes the extra solute crystallise at once.

questions.stem_md: From the curves in the chapter, the solubility of potassium nitrate at 60 degrees Celsius is closest to
questions.solution_md: Reading the red curve at 60 degrees gives the value in option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the solubility of sodium chloride in water is correct?

options.text_md: It rises steeply as the temperature rises
It falls steeply as the temperature rises
It is almost zero at every temperature
It changes very little as the temperature rises

questions.solution_md: The curve of sodium chloride is almost flat — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Crystals of potassium nitrate form when its hot saturated solution cools, because

options.text_md: its solubility becomes smaller at the lower temperature
its solubility becomes greater at the lower temperature
the water changes into potassium nitrate
cooling adds more solute to the solution

questions.solution_md: Colder water can hold less, so the excess leaves as crystals — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Calcium sulphate is highly soluble and its solubility rises steeply with temperature.
questions.solution_md: False. It is only slightly soluble and its solubility falls a little at higher temperatures.

questions.stem_md: Salt dissolves readily in water mainly because water molecules

options.text_md: are polar and pull the ions of the salt apart
are heavier than the particles of salt
react with salt to form a gas
have a lower boiling point than salt

questions.solution_md: The slightly charged ends of water molecules attract the ions — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Muddy river water is left in a jar overnight. A layer of soil collects at the bottom. The muddy water was a
questions.solution_md: Particles that settle on standing belong to a suspension — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A mixture is poured through filter paper. The filtrate is clear and the paper keeps a white residue. The mixture was most likely
questions.solution_md: Only a suspension leaves a residue on the paper — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which list puts the three kinds of mixture in order of increasing particle size?
questions.solution_md: Solution particles are smallest and suspension particles are largest — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A beam of light passing through a jar of starch paste in water appears as a bright path. This is called
questions.solution_md: Scattering of light by colloidal particles is the Tyndall effect — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Water is called the universal solvent.

**Reason (R):** Water can dissolve every substance in any amount.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true as a broad description, but the reason is false: oils, wax and sand do not dissolve — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A beam of light is visible in milk diluted with water.

**Reason (R):** The particles in a true solution are too small to scatter visible light.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Milk is a colloid and scatters light, but the reason is about true solutions, so it does not explain the milk observation — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A saturated solution of potassium nitrate at 30 degrees Celsius is heated to 50 degrees Celsius with no change in the amount of water. The solution now becomes

options.text_md: saturated, because the amount of solute is unchanged
unsaturated, because the solubility has increased
a suspension, because it is hot

questions.solution_md: The solubility of potassium nitrate rises with temperature, so the same solution can now dissolve more — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The solubility of a solid in water is correctly expressed as

options.text_md: grams of solid in 100 g of any solution
grams of solid that saturate 100 g of water at a given temperature
litres of water needed to dissolve 1 g of solid
grams of solid dissolved by any amount of water

questions.solution_md: The standard measure is the mass that saturates 100 g of water at a stated temperature — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student cools a hot saturated solution very slowly and no crystals form. A single crystal is then dropped in and many crystals form at once. The solution before the crystal was added was
questions.solution_md: Extra solute coming out at once after a crystal is added shows the solution held more than normal — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student adds salt in small portions to water at room temperature, stirring well. After the last portion a few grains stay at the bottom. The clear liquid above them is
questions.solution_md: Undissolved solid in contact with the liquid shows it can take no more — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A saturated solution can still be called a solution.

**Reason (R):** In a saturated solution the dissolved solute stays uniformly spread through the water.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true; the uniform spread explains why it is still a solution — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student heats a mixture of potassium nitrate and sodium chloride with water, then cools it. Most of the crystals that appear are those of potassium nitrate because

options.text_md: its solubility drops much more than that of sodium chloride on cooling
it is heavier than sodium chloride
sodium chloride cannot dissolve in hot water
sodium chloride dissolves more as the water cools

questions.solution_md: A steep curve means a large fall in solubility on cooling — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which statement fits the solubility curve of calcium sulphate drawn in this chapter?

options.text_md: It is very large and rises steeply
It is the same as that of sodium chloride
It is very small and falls slightly at higher temperatures
It is zero at every temperature

questions.solution_md: The curve is on its own small scale and dips at high temperature — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The solubility of potassium nitrate is 64 g per 100 g of water at 40 degrees Celsius and 169 g at 80 degrees Celsius. Heating a saturated solution from 40 to 80 degrees Celsius will let it dissolve

options.text_md: more solute, with the water unchanged

questions.solution_md: Solubility rises with temperature, so more solute can dissolve — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Using the data 32 g, 64 g, 110 g for potassium nitrate at 20, 40 and 60 degrees Celsius, the temperature at which about 64 g dissolves in 100 g of water is
questions.solution_md: Match the value to its temperature in the data — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Between 20 and 80 degrees Celsius the solubility of sodium chloride in the chapter's data changes by only 2 g, while that of potassium nitrate changes by 137 g. The better salt to purify by cooling a hot saturated solution is

options.text_md: neither, as both stay in solution

questions.solution_md: A large change in solubility gives a large mass of crystals on cooling — option (d).

questions.stem_md: At 40 degrees Celsius, 64 g of potassium nitrate saturates 100 g of water. If 50 g of potassium nitrate is stirred into 100 g of water at this temperature, the solution formed is
questions.solution_md: Fifty grams is less than the maximum, so all of it dissolves and more could dissolve — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Cooling a hot saturated solution of sodium chloride gives a large mass of crystals.

**Reason (R):** The solubility of sodium chloride changes very little with temperature.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is false: little crystallises because solubility changes so little. The reason is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A saturated solution of calcium sulphate contains very little solute.

**Reason (R):** Calcium sulphate is only slightly soluble in water.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the low solubility explains the small amount dissolved — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Name the quantity: the number of grams of a solute that saturate 100 g of water at a given temperature.

answer.model_answer_md: **Solubility.**

questions.solution_md: Solubility.

questions.stem_md: Name the effect that makes the path of a torch beam visible through a colloid.

answer.model_answer_md: **The Tyndall effect.**

questions.solution_md: Tyndall effect.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Milk, Chalk shaken in water, Sugar solution, Muddy water.

answer.model_answer_md: **Sugar solution** is the odd one out (a true solution); the other three are **mixtures whose particles scatter light or settle** (a colloid or suspensions).

questions.solution_md: Sugar solution; the rest are colloid or suspensions.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: crystals appear at once when a seed crystal is dropped into a supersaturated solution.

answer.model_answer_md: The solution holds **more solute than it normally can**, so the crystal gives the excess a place to settle and crystallise.

questions.solution_md: It holds more than it can; the crystal starts crystallisation.

questions.stem_md: State one observation when a crystal of potassium nitrate is added to a saturated solution of potassium nitrate at the same temperature.

answer.model_answer_md: The **crystal stays unchanged** and does not dissolve.

questions.solution_md: Crystal unchanged.

questions.stem_md: In a solution of copper sulphate in water, name the solute and the solvent.

answer.model_answer_md: Solute: **copper sulphate**; solvent: **water**.

questions.solution_md: Solute copper sulphate, solvent water.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: cooling a hot saturated solution of sodium chloride gives almost no crystals.

answer.model_answer_md: The **solubility of sodium chloride hardly changes** with temperature, so very little is rejected on cooling.

questions.solution_md: Its solubility is almost constant.

questions.stem_md: Name the type of mixture that is retained on filter paper and whose particles settle on standing.

answer.model_answer_md: **A suspension.**

questions.solution_md: Suspension.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A colloid settles on standing and its particles are retained by ordinary filter paper.
questions.solution_md: False. The particles of a colloid stay suspended and pass through filter paper.

questions.stem_md: True or false? For every solid, the solubility in water rises when the temperature rises.
questions.solution_md: False. Sodium chloride changes very little and calcium sulphate falls a little.

questions.stem_md: The solubility of potassium nitrate is 110 g per 100 g of water at 60 degrees Celsius. How many grams dissolve in 50 g of water to make a saturated solution at this temperature?
The solubility of sodium chloride is 36 g per 100 g of water at 20 degrees Celsius. What mass of water is needed to dissolve 90 g of sodium chloride at this temperature to make a saturated solution?
A 30 g sample of a saturated solution of salt X at 30 degrees Celsius is evaporated to dryness and leaves 6 g of solid. Calculate the solubility of X at 30 degrees Celsius in g per 100 g of water.
questions.solution_md: Water = 30 − 6 = 24 g. Solubility = 6 ÷ 24 × 100 = 25.

questions.stem_md: At 40 degrees Celsius, 64 g of potassium nitrate saturates 100 g of water. How many grams of potassium nitrate are needed to saturate 250 g of water at 40 degrees Celsius?
40 g of potassium nitrate is stirred into 50 g of water at 40 degrees Celsius, where 64 g saturates 100 g of water. What mass stays undissolved?

A saturated solution of potassium nitrate is made with 20 g of water at 80 degrees Celsius and cooled to 40 degrees Celsius. The solubility is 169 g at 80 and 64 g at 40 degrees Celsius per 100 g of water. How many grams of crystals form?

A saturated solution of potassium nitrate at 20 degrees Celsius has 32 g of the salt in every 132 g of solution. Find the mass of potassium nitrate in 100 g of the solution, correct to one decimal place.
How many grams of sodium chloride dissolve in 80 g of water at 20 degrees Celsius to give a saturated solution, if 36 g saturates 100 g of water?

Complete the paragraph with suitable terms, one for each blank. A solution that can still dissolve more solute at a given temperature is called (1) ____. A solution that has dissolved all it can at that temperature is (2) ____. A solution that holds more than that and crystallises when a crystal is added is (3) ____. The amount of solute that saturates 100 g of water is the (4) ____ of the solute. A beam of light is scattered by the particles of a colloid, which is called the (5) ____ effect.
questions.solution_md: Unsaturated; saturated; supersaturated; solubility; Tyndall.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between a true solution and a suspension on the basis of (i) settling on standing and (ii) behaviour with filter paper.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) A **solution does not settle**, while a **suspension settles** on standing. (ii) A solution **passes through** filter paper, whereas a suspension is **left behind** on it.

questions.solution_md: Settling; filter paper.

questions.stem_md: Why is water called the universal solvent? State one limitation of this name.

answer.model_answer_md: It **dissolves a wider range of substances** (solids, liquids and gases) than most other liquids. **Oil, wax or sand do not dissolve** in it.

questions.solution_md: Dissolves many; some exceptions.

marking_scheme.step: Dissolves a wide range of substances

questions.stem_md: A student has a clear solution of potassium nitrate at room temperature and wants to know if it is saturated. Describe how to find out and the observation for a saturated solution.

answer.model_answer_md: Add **one small crystal of potassium nitrate** to the solution and stir gently. If the solution is saturated, the **crystal stays unchanged**.

questions.solution_md: Add a crystal; no change.

marking_scheme.step: Adds a crystal of the same solute

questions.stem_md: A torch beam is shone through (i) a sugar solution and (ii) starch paste in water. Give the observation in each case.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **The beam is not visible** in the sugar solution. (ii) **A bright path of light is seen** in the starch paste, because the larger particles scatter light.

questions.solution_md: No beam; visible beam.

questions.stem_md: How can a supersaturated solution be made from a hot saturated solution? Why does it crystallise when disturbed?

answer.model_answer_md: Cool the hot saturated solution **slowly and without disturbing it**. It holds **more solute than it normally can**, so a knock or a crystal lets the excess crystallise.

questions.solution_md: Cool undisturbed; unstable.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between the solubility curves of potassium nitrate and sodium chloride.

answer.model_answer_md: The potassium nitrate curve **rises steeply**, while the sodium chloride curve is **almost flat**. At 80 degrees the potassium nitrate solubility is **much larger** than that of sodium chloride.

questions.solution_md: Steepness; value at high temperature.

questions.stem_md: A student says that heating a saturated solution always makes more solid dissolve. Correct the statement using the curves of potassium nitrate and calcium sulphate.

answer.model_answer_md: It is **true for potassium nitrate**, whose solubility rises with temperature, but **not for calcium sulphate**, whose solubility falls a little at higher temperatures.

questions.solution_md: Rises for potassium nitrate; falls for calcium sulphate.

questions.stem_md: The solubility of potassium nitrate at 40 degrees Celsius is 64 g per 100 g of water. Calculate the mass of the saturated solution formed from 300 g of water at 40 degrees Celsius.

answer.model_answer_md: Potassium nitrate dissolved = 64 × 300 ÷ 100 = **192 g**. Mass of solution = 300 + 192 = **492 g**.

questions.solution_md: 192 g dissolves; 492 g of solution.

questions.stem_md: 56 g of a saturated solution of salt Z is evaporated to dryness and leaves 16 g of Z. Calculate the solubility of Z in g per 100 g of water.

answer.model_answer_md: Water = 56 − 16 = **40 g**. 16 g of Z saturates 40 g of water, so for 100 g: 16 ÷ 40 × 100 = **40 g**.

questions.solution_md: Water 40 g; solubility 40 g per 100 g of water.

questions.stem_md:
The solubility of salt Y in water is 18 g per 100 g at 20 degrees Celsius, 24 g at 40 degrees Celsius and 36 g at 60 degrees Celsius.

(a) State how the solubility of Y changes with temperature and by how many grams it changes between 20 and 60 degrees Celsius. [2]

(b) Calculate the mass of Y that dissolves in 50 g of water at 60 degrees Celsius and the mass of the saturated solution. [3]

(c) The saturated solution in (b) is cooled to 20 degrees Celsius. Calculate the mass of Y that crystallises. [3]

(d) Sketch the general shape of the solubility curve of Y, labelling both axes. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The solubility **increases** with temperature, by 36 − 18 = **18 g** per 100 g of water.

**(b)** Y dissolved = 36 × 50 ÷ 100 = **18 g**; solution = 50 + 18 = **68 g**.

**(c)** At 20 degrees, 50 g of water holds 18 × 50 ÷ 100 = 9 g. Crystals = 18 − 9 = **9 g**.

**(d)** Axes: **temperature (degrees Celsius)** across and **solubility (g per 100 g of water)** up; a **rising curve** that gets steeper.

questions.solution_md: Increases, 18 g; 18 g and 68 g; 9 g; rising curve with labelled axes.

questions.stem_md:
Study the solubility graph. Curves are lettered A, B and C, and two points are lettered D and E. Curve C is drawn on its own scale.

(a) Name the salts that curves A and B are most likely to represent. [2]

(b) Point D lies on curve A at 60 degrees Celsius. State the solubility at D and the mass of the salt that saturates 250 g of water at this temperature. [3]

(c) A saturated solution at D is cooled to 20 degrees Celsius. Use the graph to find the mass of the salt that crystallises from 100 g of water. [3]

(d) Which curve belongs to the slightly soluble salt? State how its solubility changes at higher temperatures. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A: **potassium nitrate** (steep rise). B: **sodium chloride** (almost flat).

**(b)** At D the solubility is **110 g per 100 g of water**. For 250 g of water: 110 × 250 ÷ 100 = **275 g**.

**(c)** At 20 degrees the solubility is 32 g, so crystals = 110 − 32 = **78 g**.

**(d)** **Curve C** (calcium sulphate). Its solubility is very small and **falls slightly at higher temperatures**.

questions.solution_md: Potassium nitrate and sodium chloride; 110 g and 275 g; 78 g; curve C, falls slightly.

questions.stem_md:
A student prepares three liquids. Liquid X: fine sand is stirred into water. Liquid Y: potassium permanganate crystals are dissolved in water to give a clear purple liquid. Liquid Z: a little egg white is beaten into water, giving a nearly clear liquid.

(a) Name the type of mixture that each of X, Y and Z is. [3]

(b) Which liquid shows a bright path when a torch beam is shone through it from the side, but does not settle? Name the effect. [2]

(c) Which liquid will leave a residue on filter paper? [1]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the arrangement used to show the effect in (b). [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** X is a **suspension**. Y is a **solution**. Z is a **colloid**.

**(b)** **Liquid Z**. This is the **Tyndall effect**.

**(c)** **Liquid X**.

**(d)** A **torch** at the side of a **glass jar** of liquid Z, with the **beam of light** drawn crossing the liquid and a **bright path visible**; labels for torch, beam, jar and liquid.

questions.solution_md: Suspension, solution, colloid; Z, Tyndall effect; X; labelled torch and jar diagram.

(a) Name the kind of solution in each beaker. [3]

(b) Which beaker holds more dissolved salt than beaker 2 at the same temperature? Why is its solution unstable? [2]

(c) Describe how a saturated solution of the salt can be prepared and tested. [3]

**(d)** Three **beakers** with the solution level; a **dissolved crystal** in the first, an **unchanged crystal** in the second, **many crystals** in the third; labels.

questions.stem_md:
A saturated solution of potassium nitrate is made with 150 g of water at 60 degrees Celsius and then cooled to 20 degrees Celsius. At 60 and 20 degrees Celsius the solubilities are 110 g and 32 g per 100 g of water.

(a) Calculate the mass of potassium nitrate dissolved at 60 degrees Celsius. [2]

(b) Calculate the mass that the solution can hold at 20 degrees Celsius. [2]

(c) Calculate the mass of crystals that form. [2]

(d) Explain why crystals form on cooling, and why a saturated solution of sodium chloride would give almost no crystals. [2]

(e) Name the method used to separate the crystals from the liquid. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 110 × 150 ÷ 100 = **165 g**.

**(b)** 32 × 150 ÷ 100 = **48 g**.

**(c)** 165 − 48 = **117 g**.

**(d)** The **solubility of potassium nitrate falls** on cooling, so the **excess crystallises**. The solubility of **sodium chloride changes very little**, so almost nothing comes out.

**(e)** **Filtration**: the mixture is poured through filter paper, which keeps the crystals (then dried between filter papers).

questions.solution_md: 165 g; 48 g; 117 g; solubility falls; filtration.

questions.stem_md:
A student weighs a clean china dish, adds 56 g of a saturated solution of salt Z at 20 degrees Celsius and heats it gently until only dry solid is left. The mass of solid Z is 16 g.

(a) Calculate the mass of water in the sample. [1]

(b) Calculate the solubility of Z at 20 degrees Celsius in g per 100 g of water. [3]

(c) How many grams of Z are needed to saturate 250 g of water at this temperature? [2]

(d) Describe how the student should carry out the experiment and weigh the results. [3]

(e) Is a solution of 30 g of Z in 100 g of water at 20 degrees Celsius saturated? Give a reason. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 56 − 16 = **40 g**.

**(b)** 16 g saturates 40 g of water, so for 100 g: 16 ÷ 40 × 100 = **40 g per 100 g of water**.

**(c)** 40 × 250 ÷ 100 = **100 g**.

**(d)** **Weigh the empty dish**, add the solution and **weigh again**; **heat gently** to dryness, cool and **weigh the dish with the dry solid**; subtract to get the solid and the water.

**(e)** **No**, it is unsaturated, because 30 g is less than 40 g.

questions.solution_md: 40 g; 40 g per 100 g; 100 g; weighings; unsaturated.

questions.stem_md:
Study the diagram of three jars, P, Q and R, each lit from the side by a torch. The jar P is clear and the beam cannot be seen in it. In Q the beam is seen as a bright path. R is cloudy and has a layer at the bottom.

(a) Identify the type of mixture in each of P, Q and R. [3]

(b) Which jar has the largest particles and which has the smallest? [2]

(c) State which of the mixtures will pass through filter paper without leaving a residue. [2]

(d) Give one example of each mixture. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** P is a **solution**; Q is a **colloid**; R is a **suspension**.

**(b)** **R** has the largest particles and **P** the smallest.

**(c)** **P and Q** pass through filter paper (R leaves a residue).

**(d)** P: **sugar in water** (or salt). Q: **milk** or starch in water. R: **muddy water** or chalk in water.

questions.solution_md: P solution, Q colloid, R suspension; R largest, P smallest; P and Q pass; one example each.
